summary: Imperial sits on the dead-flat floor of the Imperial Valley, roughly 90 miles east of San Diego and just a few miles north of the Mexican border, where summer highs routinely push past 110°F and the landscape stretches into open-sky agricultural horizons interrupted only by irrigation canals and the distant Chocolate Mountains. That relentless sunshine — averaging 10.6 hours a day year-round — powers one of California's most productive farming regions, and agriculture, government, and healthcare (anchored by the broader El Centro metro) form the employment backbone; many residents commute the short eight-mile hop south to El Centro for work, making Imperial partly a bedroom community despite its own modest commercial corridors. At a median home price of $344,700 against a median household income of $83,214, the price-to-income ratio lands around 4.1 — strikingly affordable by California standards, where coastal metros routinely exceed 8 or 9. Median rent at $1,396 reinforces that gap. The city itself occupies just 6.3 square miles at a moderate 3,559-person-per-square-mile density, giving it a compact suburban feel with newer subdivision grids but limited walkable retail or dining clusters. Property crime sits at 263 per 100,000 and violent crime at 156, both well below California averages, with zero recorded homicides. The essential tradeoff is elemental: genuine housing affordability and wide desert skies purchased at the cost of punishing summer heat and geographic isolation from the state's larger job markets.
